I have two other major concerns that I can think of.

  • Forced updates - This is not directly related to privacy, but it is closely related. Not having the option to turn it off is a very disturbing move overall; it's the last OS vendor to make it mandatory and is a nice big step in terms of a company dictating what software you will run. This only furthers corporate interests being the real owner of the hardware that you supposedly buy. I want to have full control over the software my computer runs. And "use Professional!" is BS - I shouldn't have to pay extra for the "privlege" of controlling the computer that I own. The fact that other manufacturers do this doesn't make this right, and in fact only makes the situation considerably worse with continuous encroachment of this strategy and attitude. As a side note, this is a fantastic way to screw up your computer, and as nVidia owners found out the hard way, Microsoft's testing is pretty far from perfect, contrary to what Microsoft's fans and/or employees are saying. Also note - work-arounds are NOT ways to "turn this off," and often these will be viewed as flaws to be patched out by Microsoft, or otherwise mitigated.

  • UEFI - This is admittedly NOT part of Windows 10, but is pushed by Microsoft along with it as part of the Windows 10 debut for new computers. Furthermore, this does NOT refer to UEFI as it is was with Windows 8, as I can understand how this would be a desirable feature. Rather, the UEFI pushed with Windows 10 no longer requires the manufacturer to let it be possible to disable it. IMO this is an extremely monopolistic move and indicates that not only is Microsoft back up to their old tricks, they're also trying to make up for lost time, and quickly.

Both of these bode ill for the future of computing and consumer rights, and possibly quite a few other things (especially related to the Internet of Things) if unopposed.

Well I would say, really read up on the UEFI stuff. Here's a pretty good link:

UEFI

I think the jist is that Microsoft is allowing manufacturers, again not microsoft themselves, to allow 'only' UEFI signed OS's. So if your Dells or HP's or whatever's of the world decide to go that route I'd guess there would be a slew of people buying their PC's from someone else. Secondarily a bunch of the more mainstream distro's are already working on getting all the UEFI stuff handled, check on Ubuntu for an example.

Many people are not going to know the difference when they buy it - and a lot of people who may want to explore their computer are going to end up buying one, not even knowing about it, then want to run an alternate OS (possibly off of a boot disk/USB) but can't. This may keep people from exploring their computers as they learn about them, and can also end to hurt them in a practical situation wherein someone might want to boot an alternate OS as a recovery option. This also stifles exploration in kids - while I hate to use the "think of the children" card, it's a simple fact that a lot of people I've known over the years got their start with really learning about computers after discovering Linux when they were young teenagers, using computers their parents bought. VirtualBox just isn't the same for this sort of thing in a lot of cases, and will in any case provide a significantly diminished experience (and also will be subject to many of the same problems Windows 10 has in one way or another). Plus I'll bet that a lot of manufacturers are going to charge more for the models with a UEFI-disable option, which goes right back to the "pay extra to control your computer" problem, which is not a good road to go down, and encourages people with less money and/or knowledge to lock themselves into Windows.

Of course, all this goes out the window for tablet manufacturers, who are REQUIRED to permalock to UEFI.

In terms of allowing other OS's to be signed - that essentially allows Microsoft to be the gatekeepr as to what OS's are going to get the nod or not. Aside from being ripe for abuse, it also prevents recompilation or customization of the kernel, and strongly limits who is going to be able to get a kernel signed. I doubt, for instance, that someone who wants to start a new Linux distro will be able to do it, and in fact I'll bet that a lot of smaller or specialist distros will be able to do it. In fact, I'll bet that it's especially hard for not-for-profit OS's to get their kernels signed, such as Debian Linux, or Slackware, or Knoppix, or possibly Mint, and I'd be shocked if Kali got the nod, even for training purposes.
